Quand j'ai été converti, je n'avais jamais entendu le terme anabaptiste. Je n'avais jamais beaucoup entendu parler du témoignage auprès des autres. Je me souviens avoir pensé à tous mes amis qui ne savaient rien de ce qui venait de m'arriver. Ma petite amie de sept ans ne comprenait pas. Une chose ne cessait de me traverser l'esprit : « Je dois leur dire ! » Quelque chose de bon m'était arrivé, et tout le monde devait savoir que la même chose pouvait leur arriver ! Je me souviens d'une fois où mon frère et moi cherchions un lieu où nous pourrions parler de Jésus à beaucoup de gens. Nous avons décidé d'aller à un match de baseball de la grande ligue. J'étais nerveux, j'avais peur, et je n'oublierai jamais ce qui est arrivé. Je n'avais jamais parlé devant une grande foule auparavant, mais quand j'ai ouvert la bouche, Dieu l'a remplie.

Je n'allais pas seulement parler aux inconnus. Quand je croisais un vieil ami, je lui racontais ce qui m'était arrivé. Ils me disaient généralement qu'ils l'avaient déjà entendu et essayaient de me convaincre de me calmer et de me détendre. Je serai le premier à admettre que j'ai fait des erreurs durant ces premières années. J'ai remarqué, à ma grande surprise, que si beaucoup de gens ne m'aimaient pas, ce sont les personnes qui disaient être chrétiens qui semblaient le plus me détester. Un jour, je rendais visite à un homme âgé qui disait avoir été chrétien la majeure partie de sa vie. Pendant la discussion, il a pointé une ampoule et a dit : « Vois-tu cette ampoule ? Elle ne parle pas. » J'ai été choqué. Il me disait que oui, bien que Jésus dise que nous sommes la lumière du monde, les lampes sont censées briller silencieusement. Elles ne parlent pas.

J'étais stupéfait. Est-ce vrai ? Je suis rentré chez moi pour faire une étude biblique. Il ne fallut pas longtemps avant que je trouve des versets comme Matthieu 4:23, « Et Jésus parcourait toute la Galilée, enseignant dans leurs synagogues, prêchant la bonne nouvelle du royaume, et guérissant toute maladie et toute infirmité parmi le peuple. » Puis, en Matthieu 9, quand Jésus « vit les foules, il fut ému de compassion pour elles, parce qu'elles étaient languissantes et abattues, comme des brebis qui n'ont pas de berger. Alors il dit à ses disciples : la moisson est beaucoup, mais il y a peu d'ouvriers; priez donc le maître de la moisson qu'il envoie des ouvriers dans sa moisson » (Matthieu 9:36-38).

Il me semble que partout où Jésus allait, il parlait aux gens du royaume. J'ai vu des gens témoigner de Dieu, mais parfois d'une manière offensante. Mais cela signifie-t-il que nous ne devons pas témoigner ? Si vous lisez le livre des Actes, c'est presque tout ce que vous voyez — l'Évangile qui sort ! Dans un récit, les autorités capturèrent les disciples et dirent qu'ils pouvaient être libérés s'ils se taisaient. Cependant, les disciples dirent qu'ils ne pouvaient pas. « Car nous ne pouvons pas ne pas parler de ce que nous avons vu et entendu » (Actes 4:20). Plus tard, ils furent réduits au silence — par la mort.

Quelque temps plus tard, j'ai entendu parler de ces gens appelés anabaptistes. En les étudiant, j'ai commencé à voir comment eux aussi, ne voulaient pas se taire. J'ai commandé un exemplaire de The Martyr’s Mirror et j'ai été stupéfait quand j'ai lu ces personnes qui vivaient comme les disciples. Ils accomplissaient les paroles de Jésus : « Et vous serez haïs de tous à cause de mon nom; mais celui qui persévérera jusqu'à la fin sera sauvé » (Matt. 10:22). Et en Romains 8:36, « selon qu'il est écrit : A cause de toi nous sommes mis à mort toute la journée; nous sommes regardés comme des brebis destinées à la boucherie. »

Chers frères et sœurs, je crois que le feu s'éteint. J'entends beaucoup de nos gens anabaptistes parler de mener une vie paisible et silencieuse. Jésus nous dit dans la parabole du semeur : « Celui qui a reçu la semence parmi les épines est celui qui entend la parole; mais les soucis de ce siècle, et la séduction des richesses, étouffent la parole, et elle devient infructueuse » (Matt. 13:22). Serait-ce là où beaucoup d'entre nous en sont ? Nous vivons dans le pays libre d'Amérique où l'argent semble facile à obtenir. Est-il possible que nous ayons été trompés par notre propre richesse et par les cares de ce monde ? Sommes-nous devenus semblables au monde pour éviter d'être persécutés par lui ?

Il y a de nombreuses années, un groupe d'anabaptistes fuirent la persécution et s'installèrent dans un pays où l'oppression était moindre. Ils ouvrirent un atelier de meubles pour subvenir à leurs besoins, mais ils ne pouvaient pas vendre de meubles parce qu'ils étaient les redoutés anabaptistes. Bientôt, la situation devint désespérée car ils n'avaient pas d'argent pour acheter de la nourriture. Un jour, un homme riche entra dans l'atelier. Tous les ouvriers arrêtèrent ce qu'ils faisaient. Ils se dirent : « Peut-être que cet homme achètera quelque chose, et nous pourrons manger ! » Un vieux frère s'approcha du client potentiel et lui demanda s'il connaissait Jésus. Après une courte conversation, l'homme sortit du magasin en furie. Les ouvriers affamés demandèrent au vieil homme pourquoi il avait fait fuir leur seule chance de vente. Il expliqua que pour que cet homme connaisse Jésus, c'était bien plus important que de gagner un peu d'argent.

Dans l'esprit des premiers anabaptistes, l'Évangile de Jésus était la priorité numéro un. Comme dans les Actes, ils ne pouvaient pas ne pas parler des choses qu'ils avaient vues et entendues. Et eux aussi furent « mis à mort toute la journée ».

Alors, que faisons-nous du verset sur une vie paisible et silencieuse ? Le verset se trouve en 1 Timothée 2:1-2 : « Je recommande donc, avant toutes choses, afin qu'on fasse des supplications, des prières, des intercessions, et des actions de grâces, pour tous les hommes; pour les rois, et pour tous ceux qui sont élevés en dignité; afin que nous menions une vie paisible et tranquille, en toute piété et honnêteté. » Qu'entendait l'apôtre Paul quand il écrivit cela ? Voulait-il dire que nous devrions nous taire au sujet de l'Évangile et ne jamais remettre en question un pécheur ? Il est difficile de croire que Paul nous ordonne de faire quelque chose qu'il n'a jamais fait lui-même, quelque chose que Christ lui-même n'a jamais fait. En fait, personne dans les Écritures qui suivait Dieu ne se taisait au sujet de sa foi. Dans de nombreux récits de premiers chrétiens arrêtés pour leur foi, les autorités les suppliaient de se taire ! Mais ils refusèrent, comme le firent les disciples. Ils choisirent aussi la mort plutôt qu'une vie paisible et tranquille.

Un jeune anabaptiste arrêté laissa derrière lui sa chère épouse qui attendait leur premier enfant. Les autorités attendirent la naissance de l'enfant puis apportèrent le nourrisson au nouveau père en prison. On lui dit qu'il était maintenant père et qu'il pouvait retourner chez lui pour être avec sa femme et son fils. Il pouvait même continuer à croire de la même manière, mais il devait se taire et ne pas parler contre le péché dans l'Église d'État. Le jeune père refusa. Pour lui, se taire n'était pas une option. Ils le brûlèrent au bûcher.

Alors, que signifie 1 Timothée 2:1-2 ? Il semble que les chrétiens dans la Bible et l'Église primitive étaient entièrement consacrés à répandre l'Évangile, entièrement consacrés à l'Église du Christ. Ils allaient prêcher l'Évangile, tenant des réunions dans les montagnes, les bois, ou partout où les gens viendraient. C'était leur vie. Dans le passage de 1 Timothée 2, Paul dit que nous devons prier pour que les autorités nous permettent de vivre en paix afin que nous puissions répandre l'Évangile. Les chrétiens devraient être dehors à répandre la parole et à entrer résolument dans le royaume. Notre prière est que les autorités nous laissent vivre en paix, pendant que nous servons le Prince de la paix.

Aujourd'hui, il est facile d'être chrétien quand on s'installe et qu'on mène une vie paisible et tranquille, sans jamais remettre en question un pécheur ni corriger un frère. Mais qui a dit que ce serait facile ?

Quand nous vivions en Haïti, nous avons enseigné à notre Église le coût de suivre Jésus. C'était étonnant d'entendre les témoignages des Haïtiens appliquant l'enseignement de Jésus à leur vie. Une fois, deux membres nous dirent qu'ils allaient perdre leur emploi à cause de leur fidélité à l'Évangile. Les entendre prendre position pour la vérité me réjouissait. Une autre sœur de l'Église me dit que l'école où allaient ses enfants imposait des uniformes et que les filles devaient porter des pantalons. Quand elle envoya sa fille à l'école vêtue d'une robe modeste, elle revint avec une note du directeur disant qu'elle ne devait pas revenir à l'école vêtue de cette chose.

1 Pierre 4:14 dit : « Si vous êtes outragés à cause du nom du Christ, vous êtes heureux; car l'esprit de gloire, et l'Esprit de Dieu, repose sur vous; de la part des autres il est blâmé, mais de votre part il est glorifié. »

La vraie joie vient de la souffrance. La souffrance vient de l'obéissance à Jésus. Sommes-nous trop occupés par des choses futiles pendant que le monde va en enfer ? Suivons Jésus comme les premiers chrétiens, où personne ne pouvait nier que la puissance de Dieu agissait en eux. Nous avons quelque chose dont tout le monde a besoin. Qu'attendons-nous ? Rassemblons-nous à nouveau, réunissons-nous, renions-nous nous-mêmes, prenons la croix, et suivons-Le !

Greetings in the worthy name of the Lord Jesus Christ. As I gaze out across the barren January landscape, I can’t help but wonder what this new year will bring. Undoubtedly, it will bring a mixture of joy and sorrow, excitement and drear, laughter and tears, and everything else in between, which only an Almighty Creator God can arrange in such a way that will magnify His worthy power and excellence. Yet our finite, negative minds tend to anticipate all the bad things that could happen. Will inflation drive food prices even higher? Will widespread fighting erupt across the Middle East? What will happen in the elections? Will the losing party resort to protests and rioting?

I suppose, since the fall of man, these fear-driven thoughts have roamed through the minds of humanity at the beginning of each year. Yet, as it is so aptly pointed out by the writer of the article, “God’s Faithfulness Manifest Even in the Curse”, God has kindly provided for humanity since the beginning of time. Looking back at God’s faithfulness to man over the centuries, we have no reason to doubt God will do the same for us in 2024.

Despite God’s faithfulness to us, the effects of the fall of man are still evident. Family members get sick, church and relationship struggles rob us of sleep, the checkbook runs dry, the children squabble and cry, and the demands of our schedules have us hopping from one event to the next. And sometimes, it seems that all these calamities hit us at the same time. Our bodies and minds are not created to handle this. We become weary. Bone tired. Exhausted to the point when even thinking hurts. We face burnout. In this issue, “A Word From the Doctor” guides us as we face the maze of life, giving us practical and Biblical solutions to avoid or recover from burnout. He writes, “Jesus knows our limitations. He wants us to have balance, living in such a way that we not only have strength for today but also for tomorrow, next week, and next year – till He comes again.”

Perhaps one good remedy to reduce the stress of life would be to go for a bike ride. But we need to be careful and avoid getting into a bike race like the two lads did in this issue’s children’s story. We may end up with more stress than we bargained for.

Despite our best efforts to live stress-free lives, we still meet with the unexpected. Last week I was cleaning out our broiler houses in preparation for a new flock. I leaned across the tractor fender to push a partly opened door out of the way. As I stood up, my foot accidentally hit the hydrostatic pedal, lurching the tractor forward and throwing me off-balance. My foot somehow got caught under the pedal, and for a split second, I feared I would fall right in front of the rear wheel. In a last-ditch effort, I threw myself away from the tractor. My foot slipped out of my shoe, and I landed unharmed on the ground. The tractor slowly headed off with my shoe still wedged under the pedal. All ended well, and a few lessons were learned. It was nothing other than the providence of God that prevented a freak incident from becoming a bad accident. Truly I agree with Solomon, “For the LORD shall be thy confidence, and shall keep thy foot from being taken” (Proverbs 3:26).

As we navigate through this year, let’s join the hymnwriter in worship, where he writes:

When all Thy mercies, O my God,
My rising soul surveys,
Transported with the view, I’m lost
In wonder, love and praise.

It is only by the mercies of an all-loving God that we have life and breath. May we give our all to Him and to the work of His kingdom in heartfelt thanksgiving for His unspeakable gift.

Blessings to all,

Edward Martin

奉配得尊名的主耶稣基督的名向你们致意。当我眺望一片荒凉的一月景色时，不禁想知道这一新年将带来什么。毫无疑问，它会带来喜乐与悲伤并存、兴奋与沉闷交织、欢笑与眼泪相伴，以及其他一切，唯有全能的创造主才能以这样的方式安排，使祂的尊贵大能和卓越得到彰显。然而，我们有限且消极的心思往往预期所有可能发生的不幸。通货膨胀会把食物价格推得更高吗？中东会爆发大规模冲突吗？选举会发生什么？落败的一方会诉诸抗议和暴乱吗？

自从人的堕落以来，我想这些源于恐惧的念头在每年年初常常游走在人类心中。然而，正如题为“即使在咒诅中，上帝的信实仍然显明”的文章作者恰当地指出，从创世以来，上帝就亲切地供应人类。回顾数世纪间上帝对人的信实，我们没有理由怀疑上帝在 2024 年也会为我们如此行。

尽管上帝对我们信实，人的堕落后果仍然显而易见。家人得病，教会与人际关系的挣扎使我们失眠，支票簿见底，孩子们争吵哭闹，日程的要求使我们在一个活动与下一个活动之间匆忙奔波。有时，似乎所有这些灾难同时降临。我们的身心并非为此而造。我们变得疲惫不堪，筋疲力尽，疲惫到连思考都痛苦。我们面临精疲力竭。在本期中，“医生的嘱咐”（A Word From the Doctor）在我们面对人生迷宫时为我们指引，提供切实且合乎圣经的方案以避免或恢复倦怠。他写道：“耶稣知道我们的限度。祂要我们有平衡的生活，使我们不仅有今日的力量，也有明天、下周和来年的力量——直到祂再来。”

也许减轻生活压力的一个好方法是去骑自行车。但我们需要小心，避免像本期儿童故事里的两个小伙子那样陷入自行车竞赛。我们可能会因此招致比预期更多的压力。

尽管我们尽力过无压力的生活，意外仍会发生。上周我在为新一批鸡群准备时清理育雏舍。我靠在拖拉机挡泥板上，将半开的门推到一边。站起身时，我的脚不小心碰到了液压踏板，拖拉机猛地向前冲，把我顶得失去平衡。我的脚不知怎么被踏板卡住，瞬间我害怕自己会跌到后轮前面。最后一刻，我拼命往远处一扑。我的脚从鞋里滑出，我毫发无伤地落在地上。拖拉机慢慢开走，鞋仍然楔在踏板下。一切以平安结束，我也学到几课。若非上帝的眷顾，这次意外的事故本可能变成严重的伤害。我确实同意所罗门的话：“因为耶和华必成为你的信靠，并要保守你的脚不被夺走”（箴言 3:26）。

在我们走过这一年时，让我们与诗歌作者一同敬拜，他写道：

当我主诸般怜悯显现在我眼前，
我高升的灵魂审视这一切，
被这景象感动，我迷失其中，
在奇异、爱与赞美里沉醉。

惟有全然慈爱的上帝的怜悯，我们才有生命和气息。愿我们为祂和祂国的工献上全部，以感恩的心为祂那无法言说的恩赐献上衷心的感谢。

愿众蒙赐福，

Edward Martin

Prayer lays hold of God's plan and becomes the link between His will and its accomplishment on earth. Amazing things happen, and we are given the privilege of being the channels of the Holy Spirit's prayer.

—Elisabeth Elliot

In May 2001, God blessed our family with a baby girl. This baby created a lot of excitement as the news flew like wildfire. “Did you hear Ivans have a girl?” Her only sister was 14 years old, and the last five babies had been boys. Such a special baby deserved a special name. We named her Judith Irene after her grandmother and called her Judy for short.

The first 24 hours after birth, Judy grunted and squawked almost continuously. “She is disgruntled about being born,” I joked. After that first day she settled into a normal baby routine with no sign of anything unordinary.

One morning when Judy was about 18 months old, I was in the living room having my personal devotions. She was in the adjoining kitchen when we heard an odd noise—a rhythmical scratch-thunk. I looked quizzically at Ivan. “What is that noise?” With raised eyebrows, he shrugged his shoulders. When the sounds continued, I got curious enough to heft myself out of my rocking chair and trudge toward the source of the sounds. An uneasy suspicion reared its head in the back of my mind and grew with every step I took. When I entered the kitchen, Judy lay on the floor, jerking rhythmically. I had never seen anyone in a seizure before, but somehow, I just knew. She’s having a seizure!

“Shall we call 911?” Ivan headed toward the phone. I debated. Since Ivan was a firefighter, we had an emergency scanner in the house. After hearing countless calls over the years and knowing it could sometimes take the ambulance a while to respond, I wasn't at rest waiting at home while our daughter was seizing.

“Let’s take her in.” I wasn’t willing to sit there and wait until help arrived.

Judy was still jerking. Ivan scooped her off the floor and handed her to me so he could get his keys. Holding Judy close, I headed for the door. “Bring my shoes,” I called over my shoulder as I hurried stocking-footed down the porch steps and toward the pickup truck parked in the lower driveway. Ivan passed me up, opened the door for me, and ran around to the driver’s side. Coming down the short, steep hill, my feet slipped in the morning dew, and I landed halfway under the truck with one leg forward and the other one bent back under me. For an instant, I thought I had broken my leg, but after a stunned second or two, I got to my feet, gathered my precious burden, and struggled into the pickup. Judy was still jerking and, worse yet, was no longer breathing properly. Saliva pooled in the corners of her mouth, turning into foam. Oh my baby! What is wrong with her? Is she going to die?! It’s amazing how many thoughts can run through your mind in a situation like this. Why, oh why doesn’t Ivan drive faster? She’s not breathing! I glanced over at the speedometer. It was pointed hard right. Oh, he was driving fast. With my whole body and mind, I willed us to be at the hospital.

We had a straight drive to the hospital, and Ivan pulled right up to the emergency entrance. I jumped out of the truck with my baby, yelled over my shoulder to bring my shoes along in, and ran for the emergency door. A nurse was just coming around the corner and I all but threw my precious baby into her startled arms. “She’s having a seizure!” I squeaked out. The nurse took one look at Judy, turned, and rushed down the hall with me at her heels. By the time we got into a room, Judy had finally stopped seizing. As she lay on the stretcher, semi-comatose, she went into a second, milder seizure.

Once she came out of the second seizure and things calmed down, the doctor ordered some tests. After reviewing the test results, the doctor decided she had experienced a febrile seizure, one that results from body temperature moving up or down too rapidly. He said they were common in babies and young children and didn’t seem too concerned. My mothering instincts questioned his diagnosis, but I was no doctor so we went with what he said.

This was our introduction to the world of seizures. A few weeks later she had another seizure. And then another. Our parents encouraged us to get a second opinion. This second doctor decided that Judy should have an MRI, even though the first doctor still maintained that she was just having febrile seizures and wasn’t in any hurry to do the MRI. Several weeks passed until they worked her into the schedule. The day after the MRI, we got a call from the doctor’s office. An appointment with a neurosurgeon had been made for two days later. The situation had changed from “no hurry” to “you will be there, no questions asked”. The neurosurgeon said Judy had an AVM and tried to explain what that was, but most of the information soared right over my head. An appointment for an angiogram was scheduled, and explanations of procedures and requirements for us as her parents were added to my spinning brain. As I tried to digest all the information I was receiving in one phone call, I realized they were preparing for the possibility of surgery.

Our prayers were getting more earnest as we progressed through an EEG (brain scan looking for seizure activity) and more doctor visits. We desired healing for our baby so she could live a normal life. Our faith in God came into play as we tried to resign ourselves to His will. Friends, family, and acquaintances all joined us in prayer.

We owned a bulk food store, and many local non-Mennonite folks knew us. We had become good friends with some Christians from a local church. When they heard of the circumstances, they asked if they could have a prayer meeting to lay hands on Judy and pray for her healing. Although the church we attended did not generally do this, we appreciated their sincerity and faith in God, so we agreed to it.

The evening came when we gathered at their church with their pastor and some of the members who knew us. They took turns praying and claimed God’s healing for Judy because they “knew” it was His will to heal her. They specifically asked that the doctors wouldn’t find anything when they did the angiogram. Then they asked us to pray. Although not used to praying out loud, particularly in front of other people, we had confidence that God could heal our baby and wanted to do our part. We prayed for God’s will and voiced our acceptance of whatever He chose.

The next day, we made the hour-and-a-half drive to Madison Children’s Hospital for the angiogram. The purpose for this test was to identify what was causing her seizures and to find its exact location. After the test, we went home to await the results.

I didn’t want my lack of faith to block my daughter’s healing, and I knew God could heal her, but who was I to tell Him what to do? As I struggled through it, we waited for news from the doctor.

Two days later we got a phone call from the doctor’s office. The nurse on the line told us the angiogram hadn’t shown anything! It seemed to puzzle them. It wasn’t at all what they had expected, and they didn’t understand why they couldn’t find the problem. Praise God! We marveled at the miracle He had wrought.

When we took Judy to her next appointment with the neurosurgeon, I asked him what Judy’s problem was since the angiogram found nothing unusual. He said it appeared she had a small amount of bleeding on her brain, but not to worry about it. I thought that was one of the strangest statements I ever heard. I had always been under the impression that bleeding on the brain is very serious and not to be ignored. But I was pretty sure I knew what had happened and told the doctor about the prayers. His response was noncommittal, and I couldn’t tell what he really thought.

They scheduled Judy for a second doctor’s visit and MRI in six months, which I thought was a little strange, considering that they didn’t think there was anything wrong with her. I wasn’t planning to need that MRI or appointment since I believed God had healed her.

That summer, we weaned her off her seizure medications, and she appeared to be healthy. The six months were almost over, and we believed her problems were behind us.

Then, one week before the scheduled MRI, she had a seizure. What a shock! How could this be? Hadn’t God healed her?? What was happening? I felt betrayed. All I could ask was, “Why?” And now what were we going to do?

Such emotional turmoil and soul-searching! I felt let down and shaken in my faith. I had believed in God and that was finally where I ended up every time when I struggled. Solid as a rock under all the turmoil was the truth that God is, and His ways are far above my understanding. I found at the core of my belief in God a safe place where He knows and has my best interest in mind. And that plan might not include the things I want to happen in my limited earth-view.

What if His plan was higher? What if there was someone we would encounter through our medical journey who needed to see Christ in us? Were we willing to be His witness at the expense of our comfort and an easier life?

Our precious little girl ended up having brain surgery at only three and a half years old. Dealing with seizures, surgery, and countless tests over the years caused us no small amount of stress, but God had and still has a plan, and the “whys” we ask might not be revealed until we see Him face to face.

So, does God always answer prayer? I say yes, He does. Sometimes He says, “Yes,” and we get what we want; sometimes, His answer is“No,” and we do not get what we ask for. Sometimes, He whispers, “Wait”, and in His own time and way, He allows us our heart’s desire. Like a child who trusts his parents, I will leave the answers to my prayers in the hands of our almighty God and trust Him to know what is best for my life.

A oração toma posse do plano de Deus e torna-se o elo entre a Sua vontade e a sua realização na terra. Coisas maravilhosas acontecem, e temos o privilégio de ser os canais da oração do Espírito Santo.

—Elisabeth Elliot

Em maio de 2001, Deus abençoou nossa família com uma menina. Esse bebê causou muita excitação enquanto a notícia se espalhava como fogo selvagem. “Você ouviu que os Ivans tiveram uma menina?” A única irmã dela tinha 14 anos, e os cinco últimos bebês tinham sido meninos. Um bebê tão especial merecia um nome especial. Batizamos-na de Judith Irene, em homenagem à avó, e a chamávamos de Judy, de forma abreviada.

Nas primeiras 24 horas após o nascimento, Judy resmungou e grasnou quase continuamente. “Ela está aborrecida por ter nascido”, brinquei. Depois desse primeiro dia ela entrou numa rotina normal de bebê, sem sinal de nada fora do comum.

Certa manhã, quando Judy tinha cerca de 18 meses, eu estava na sala fazendo meu devocional pessoal. Ela estava na cozinha ao lado quando ouvimos um ruído estranho — um arranhado-choque rítmico. Olhei para Ivan com curiosidade. “Que é esse barulho?” Com as sobrancelhas erguidas, ele deu de ombros. Quando os sons continuaram, fiquei curiosa o bastante para me levantar da cadeira de balanço e caminhar em direção à fonte do ruído. Uma suspeita inquietante brotou na minha mente e cresceu a cada passo que eu dava. Ao entrar na cozinha, Judy jazia no chão, contraindo-se ritmicamente. Eu nunca tinha visto ninguém ter uma convulsão antes, mas de alguma forma eu simplesmente soube. Ela está tendo uma convulsão!

“Devemos ligar para o 911?” Ivan se dirigiu ao telefone. Eu hesitei. Como Ivan era bombeiro, tínhamos um rádio de emergência em casa. Depois de ouvir inúmeras chamadas ao longo dos anos e sabendo que às vezes a ambulância pode demorar a chegar, eu não fiquei tranquila esperando em casa enquanto nossa filha tinha convulsões.

“Vamos levá-la.” Eu não estava disposta a ficar sentada e esperar até que chegasse ajuda.

Judy ainda se contraía. Ivan a pegou do chão e me entregou para ir buscar as chaves. Segurando Judy bem junto, fui em direção à porta. “Traga meus sapatos,” gritei por cima do ombro enquanto descia apressada os degraus da varanda de meia sola e caminhava em direção ao caminhão estacionado na entrada inferior. Ivan me ultrapassou, abriu a porta para mim e correu para o lado do motorista. Descendo a ladeira curta e íngreme, meus pés escorregaram no orvalho da manhã e eu caí até metade por baixo do caminhão com uma perna para frente e a outra dobrada para trás sob mim. Por um instante pensei que tinha quebrado a perna, mas depois de um segundo ou dois atordoada, levantei-me, recolhi meu precioso fardo e me debati para entrar no caminhão. Judy ainda se contraía e, pior, já não respirava corretamente. Saliva se acumulava nos cantos da boca, transformando-se em espuma. Oh, minha bebê! O que há de errado com ela? Será que vai morrer?! É impressionante quantos pensamentos podem passar pela sua mente numa situação assim. Por que, oh por que, Ivan não dirige mais rápido? Ela não está respirando! Olhei para o velocímetro. Ele estava totalmente à direita. Oh, ele estava dirigindo rápido. Com todo meu corpo e mente, desejei que estivéssemos no hospital.

Tivemos um trajeto direto até o hospital, e Ivan parou bem na entrada da emergência. Saltei do caminhão com minha bebê, gritei por cima do ombro para trazer meus sapatos junto e corri para a porta da emergência. Uma enfermeira estava justamente contornando a esquina e eu quase lancei minha preciosa bebê em seus braços assustados. “Ela está tendo uma convulsão!” consegui dizer num fio de voz. A enfermeira olhou rapidamente para Judy, virou-se e correu pelo corredor com eu a seus calcanhares. Quando chegamos a uma sala, Judy finalmente havia parado de se contrair. Enquanto jazia na maca, semi-comatosa, ela entrou em uma segunda convulsão, mais leve.

Quando ela saiu da segunda convulsão e as coisas se acalmaram, o médico pediu alguns exames. Após analisar os resultados, ele decidiu que ela havia tido uma convulsão febril, uma que decorre de a temperatura do corpo subir ou descer muito rapidamente. Disse que eram comuns em bebês e crianças pequenas e não parecia muito preocupado. Meus instintos maternos questionaram seu diagnóstico, mas eu não era médica, então seguimos o que ele disse.

Essa foi nossa introdução ao mundo das convulsões. Algumas semanas depois ela teve outra convulsão. E depois outra. Nossos pais nos incentivaram a buscar uma segunda opinião. Esse segundo médico decidiu que Judy deveria fazer uma ressonância magnética, embora o primeiro médico ainda sustentasse que ela estava apenas tendo convulsões febris e não tivesse pressa em realizar a ressonância. Passaram-se várias semanas até que a incluíssem na agenda. No dia seguinte à ressonância, recebemos uma ligação do consultório. Uma consulta com um neurocirurgião foi marcada para dois dias depois. A situação havia mudado de “sem pressa” para “vocês vão estar lá, sem perguntas”. O neurocirurgião disse que Judy tinha uma MAV e tentou explicar o que era, mas a maior parte da informação passou por cima da minha cabeça. Foi agendada uma angiografia, e explicações sobre procedimentos e exigências para nós como pais se acumularam na minha mente atordoada. Enquanto tentava digerir todas as informações que recebia numa única ligação, percebi que eles estavam se preparando para a possibilidade de cirurgia.

Nossas orações tornaram-se mais fervorosas enquanto passávamos por um EEG (eletroencefalograma, exame do cérebro para detectar atividade convulsiva) e por mais consultas médicas. Desejávamos a cura para nossa bebê para que ela pudesse viver uma vida normal. Nossa fé em Deus entrou em cena enquanto tentávamos nos resignar à Sua vontade. Amigos, família e conhecidos se uniram a nós em oração.

Nós tínhamos uma mercearia a granel, e muitos locais não menonitas nos conheciam. Havíamos feito boas amizades com alguns cristãos de uma igreja local. Quando souberam das circunstâncias, perguntaram se poderiam fazer uma reunião de oração para impor as mãos em Judy e orar por sua cura. Embora a igreja que frequentávamos geralmente não fizesse isso, apreciamos a sinceridade e a fé deles em Deus, então concordamos.

Certa noite nos reunimos na igreja deles com o pastor e alguns membros que nos conheciam. Eles oraram por turnos e reivindicaram a cura de Deus para Judy porque “sabiam” que era vontade dEle curá-la. Pediram especificamente que os médicos não encontrassem nada quando fizessem a angiografia. Depois pediram que nós orássemos. Embora não acostumados a orar em voz alta, especialmente na frente de outras pessoas, tínhamos confiança de que Deus podia curar nossa bebê e queríamos fazer nossa parte. Oramos pela vontade de Deus e expressamos nossa aceitação de tudo o que Ele escolhesse.

No dia seguinte, fizemos a viagem de uma hora e meia até o Madison Children’s Hospital para a angiografia. O propósito desse exame era identificar o que estava causando as convulsões e localizar com precisão. Após o exame, voltamos para casa para aguardar os resultados.

Eu não queria que minha falta de fé impedisse a cura de minha filha, e eu sabia que Deus podia curá-la, mas quem era eu para dizer a Ele o que fazer? Enquanto lutava com isso, aguardamos notícias do médico.

Dois dias depois, recebemos uma ligação do consultório. A enfermeira informou que a angiografia não tinha mostrado nada! Parecia deixá-los perplexos. Não era o que esperavam, e eles não compreendiam por que não conseguiam encontrar o problema. Louvemos a Deus! Admiramos o milagre que Ele realizara.

Quando levamos Judy à consulta seguinte com o neurocirurgião, perguntei o que era o problema dela, já que a angiografia não encontrou nada de anormal. Ele disse que parecia haver uma pequena quantidade de sangramento no cérebro, mas que não nos preocupássemos. Achei essa uma das afirmações mais estranhas que já ouvi. Sempre tive a impressão de que hemorragia cerebral é muito séria e não deve ser ignorada. Mas eu estava bastante certa de saber o que havia acontecido e contei ao médico sobre as orações. A resposta dele foi não comprometida, e eu não consegui entender o que ele realmente pensava.

Agendaram uma segunda consulta e outra ressonância magnética para daqui a seis meses, o que me pareceu um pouco estranho, considerando que eles não achavam que houvesse algo de errado com ela. Eu não planejava precisar daquela ressonância ou daquela consulta, já que acreditava que Deus a havia curado.

Aquele verão a desmamamos dos medicamentos anticonvulsivantes e ela parecia saudável. Os seis meses estavam quase passando, e acreditávamos que os problemas haviam ficado para trás.

Então, uma semana antes da ressonância marcada, ela teve uma convulsão. Que choque! Como isso podia ser? Deus não a havia curado? O que estava acontecendo? Senti-me traída. Tudo o que pude perguntar foi: “Por quê?” E agora o que íamos fazer?

Que tormento emocional e busca interior! Senti-me desapontada e abalada na fé. Eu havia creído em Deus e era sempre ali que eu acabava quando lutava. Sólido como uma rocha em meio a todo o tumulto era o fato de que Deus existe, e os Seus caminhos estão muito acima da minha compreensão. Encontrei, no cerne da minha crença em Deus, um lugar seguro onde Ele conhece e tem em mente o meu melhor interesse. E esse plano talvez não inclua as coisas que eu quero que aconteçam na minha visão limitada da terra.

E se o plano dEle fosse mais elevado? E se houvesse alguém que encontraríamos ao longo da nossa jornada médica que precisasse ver Cristo em nós? Estaríamos dispostos a ser Seu testemunho à custa do nosso conforto e de uma vida mais fácil?

Nossa preciosa filhinha acabou fazendo uma cirurgia no cérebro com apenas três anos e meio. Lidar com convulsões, cirurgia e inúmeros exames ao longo dos anos nos causou uma quantia considerável de estresse, mas Deus tinha e ainda tem um plano, e os “por quês” que perguntamos podem não ser revelados até que o vejamos face a face.

Então, Deus sempre responde à oração? Eu digo que sim, Ele responde. Às vezes Ele diz “Sim”, e recebemos o que queremos; às vezes, Sua resposta é “Não”, e não recebemos o que pedimos. Às vezes, Ele sussurra “Espere”, e, ao Seu tempo e modo, Ele nos permite o desejo do nosso coração. Como uma criança que confia nos pais, deixarei as respostas às minhas orações nas mãos do nosso Deus todo-poderoso e confiarei que Ele sabe o que é melhor para a minha vida.

It was one of those Sunday afternoons in late spring when the sun was finally shining warmly. It was the time of year when little boys seem to have plenty of extra energy. Little Davy was sitting on the road bank with some neighborhood boys who had stopped by. He felt like jumping up and down in anticipation of the upcoming race.

Two older boys, Big David and Paul, showed up with brand-new bicycles. These were not the ordinary bicycles the other boys had. They were beautiful Vista bicycles with gleaming new paint, shiny chrome fenders, and three speeds. These bicycles glided smoothly on the chip-and seal road without a rattle. With new ball bearings, they whizzed along with hardly any effort being applied to the pedals. Even though there did not seem to be much difference between the bicycles, Big David’s was a gleaming chestnut brown, and Paul’s a sparkling metal flake blue.

“Well,” Big David began to brag, “With my longer legs, and freshly sprayed WD40, my bike is sure to be the fastest.”

“No,” challenged Paul, “my shorter legs can pump faster, and Schwinn’s high-test bicycle oil by far outperforms WD40, which really is only for squeaks.”

“A race! A race!” the other boys said, “Why not settle it with a race?”

“Okay,” Big David said, “We’ll have a race and see whose bike is really the fastest.”

“You bet!” Paul agreed. “We’ll start at the top of Billy’s hill and race all the way down to the bottom,” he said, pointing to the road bank where the other boys were sitting.

One, two, three, GO and they were off! Down the hill they came, pedaling for all they were worth.

“Go Paul!” and “Go Big David!” shouted the boys at the bottom of the hill. All the commotion woke up Little Davy’s rat terrier dog, Nellie. Yapping loudly, Nellie zoomed around the silo as fast as her four little legs could carry her. She headed straight for Big David’s bicycle in the front, barking loudly to try to make it stop. Poor Nellie did not realize another bicycle was trying to pass up the first one.

Thump, the passing bicycle hit the dog! Crash, bang, the two bicycles ran into each other!

“Hey – aye!” Oooff! Two boys flew over the handlebars and landed hard on the road. Those shining bicycles were no longer gleaming. They were lying on a heap, scratched and streaked with tar. Nellie limped back beside the silo and stayed lying there for several hours.

The other boys stood on the bank with their mouths open. Quickly, they ran to the two big boys lying by their new bicycles. “Are you okay?” they asked.

“I’ll be okay,” Paul said slowly, “but no more races. Who even cares whose bike is the fastest.”

Even though Little Davy is now a grandpa, he has not forgotten the bicycle race on that long ago Sunday afternoon, when Big David and Paul learned that bragging and showing off usually comes to a crashing end.

Fue una de esas tardes de domingo a finales de la primavera en que el sol por fin brillaba cálido. Era la época del año en que a los niños pequeños parece que les sobra energía. El pequeño Davy estaba sentado en la cuneta de la carretera con algunos niños del vecindario que se habían detenido. Tenía ganas de saltar de arriba abajo anticipando la carrera que se avecinaba.

Aparecieron dos chicos mayores, Big David y Paul, con bicicletas nuevas de paquete. No eran las bicicletas ordinarias que tenían los otros niños. Eran hermosas bicicletas Vista con pintura nueva reluciente, guardabarros cromados y tres velocidades. Estas bicicletas se deslizaban sin vibrar por la carretera sellada con gravilla. Con rodamientos nuevos, corrían casi sin esfuerzo al aplicar los pedales. Aunque no parecía haber mucha diferencia entre las bicicletas, la de Big David era de un brillante color castaño avellana y la de Paul de un azul metalizado con purpurina.

“Bueno,” comenzó a presumir Big David, “con mis piernas más largas y el WD40 recién rociado, mi bici seguro que será la más rápida.”

“No,” replicó Paul, “mis piernas más cortas pueden pedalear más rápido, y el aceite de alta resistencia para bicicletas de Schwinn supera con creces al WD40, que en realidad es solo para chirridos.”

“¡Una carrera! ¡Una carrera!” dijeron los otros chicos, “¿Por qué no lo arreglamos con una carrera?”

“Está bien,” dijo Big David, “Haremos una carrera y veremos cuál bicicleta es realmente la más rápida.”

“¡Apuesto!” estuvo de acuerdo Paul. “Empezaremos en la cima de la colina de Billy y competiremos hasta el fondo,” dijo, señalando la cuneta donde estaban sentados los otros chicos.

¡Uno, dos, tres, YA! y salieron disparados. Bajaron la colina pedaleando con todas sus fuerzas.

“¡Vamos Paul!” y “¡Vamos Big David!” gritaban los chicos al pie de la colina. Todo el alboroto despertó a la perrita rat terrier del pequeño Davy, Nellie. Ladrando fuerte, Nellie dio vueltas alrededor del silo tan deprisa como sus cuatro patitas se lo permitían. Se dirigió directamente hacia la bicicleta de Big David al frente, ladrando para intentar detenerla. La pobre Nellie no se dio cuenta de que otra bicicleta iba a adelantar a la primera.

¡Plaf!, la bicicleta que adelantaba golpeó al perro. ¡Crash, bang!, las dos bicicletas chocaron entre sí.

“¡Eh – ay!” ¡Uff! Dos chicos salieron volando por encima del manillar y cayeron con fuerza sobre la carretera. Aquellas bicicletas relucientes ya no brillaban. Yacían amontonadas, arañadas y con rayas de alquitrán. Nellie cojeó de regreso junto al silo y se quedó tumbada allí varias horas.

Los otros chicos se quedaron en la cuneta con la boca abierta. Rápidamente corrieron hacia los dos chicos mayores que yacían junto a sus bicicletas nuevas. “¿Están bien?” preguntaron.

“Estaré bien,” dijo Paul lentamente, “pero nada de más carreras. A quién le importa cuál bici es la más rápida.”

Aunque el pequeño Davy ahora es abuelo, no ha olvidado la carrera de bicicletas de aquella tarde de domingo hace tanto tiempo, cuando Big David y Paul aprendieron que presumir y alardear suele acabar en un estrepitoso fracaso.

Prayer lays hold of God's plan and becomes the link between His will and its accomplishment on earth. Amazing things happen, and we are given the privilege of being the channels of the Holy Spirit's prayer.

—Elisabeth Elliot

In May 2001, God blessed our family with a baby girl. This baby created a lot of excitement as the news flew like wildfire. “Did you hear Ivans have a girl?” Her only sister was 14 years old, and the last five babies had been boys. Such a special baby deserved a special name. We named her Judith Irene after her grandmother and called her Judy for short.

The first 24 hours after birth, Judy grunted and squawked almost continuously. “She is disgruntled about being born,” I joked. After that first day she settled into a normal baby routine with no sign of anything unordinary.

One morning when Judy was about 18 months old, I was in the living room having my personal devotions. She was in the adjoining kitchen when we heard an odd noise—a rhythmical scratch-thunk. I looked quizzically at Ivan. “What is that noise?” With raised eyebrows, he shrugged his shoulders. When the sounds continued, I got curious enough to heft myself out of my rocking chair and trudge toward the source of the sounds. An uneasy suspicion reared its head in the back of my mind and grew with every step I took. When I entered the kitchen, Judy lay on the floor, jerking rhythmically. I had never seen anyone in a seizure before, but somehow, I just knew. She’s having a seizure!

“Shall we call 911?” Ivan headed toward the phone. I debated. Since Ivan was a firefighter, we had an emergency scanner in the house. After hearing countless calls over the years and knowing it could sometimes take the ambulance a while to respond, I wasn't at rest waiting at home while our daughter was seizing.

“Let’s take her in.” I wasn’t willing to sit there and wait until help arrived.

Judy was still jerking. Ivan scooped her off the floor and handed her to me so he could get his keys. Holding Judy close, I headed for the door. “Bring my shoes,” I called over my shoulder as I hurried stocking-footed down the porch steps and toward the pickup truck parked in the lower driveway. Ivan passed me up, opened the door for me, and ran around to the driver’s side. Coming down the short, steep hill, my feet slipped in the morning dew, and I landed halfway under the truck with one leg forward and the other one bent back under me. For an instant, I thought I had broken my leg, but after a stunned second or two, I got to my feet, gathered my precious burden, and struggled into the pickup. Judy was still jerking and, worse yet, was no longer breathing properly. Saliva pooled in the corners of her mouth, turning into foam. Oh my baby! What is wrong with her? Is she going to die?! It’s amazing how many thoughts can run through your mind in a situation like this. Why, oh why doesn’t Ivan drive faster? She’s not breathing! I glanced over at the speedometer. It was pointed hard right. Oh, he was driving fast. With my whole body and mind, I willed us to be at the hospital.

We had a straight drive to the hospital, and Ivan pulled right up to the emergency entrance. I jumped out of the truck with my baby, yelled over my shoulder to bring my shoes along in, and ran for the emergency door. A nurse was just coming around the corner and I all but threw my precious baby into her startled arms. “She’s having a seizure!” I squeaked out. The nurse took one look at Judy, turned, and rushed down the hall with me at her heels. By the time we got into a room, Judy had finally stopped seizing. As she lay on the stretcher, semi-comatose, she went into a second, milder seizure.

Once she came out of the second seizure and things calmed down, the doctor ordered some tests. After reviewing the test results, the doctor decided she had experienced a febrile seizure, one that results from body temperature moving up or down too rapidly. He said they were common in babies and young children and didn’t seem too concerned. My mothering instincts questioned his diagnosis, but I was no doctor so we went with what he said.

This was our introduction to the world of seizures. A few weeks later she had another seizure. And then another. Our parents encouraged us to get a second opinion. This second doctor decided that Judy should have an MRI, even though the first doctor still maintained that she was just having febrile seizures and wasn’t in any hurry to do the MRI. Several weeks passed until they worked her into the schedule. The day after the MRI, we got a call from the doctor’s office. An appointment with a neurosurgeon had been made for two days later. The situation had changed from “no hurry” to “you will be there, no questions asked”. The neurosurgeon said Judy had an AVM and tried to explain what that was, but most of the information soared right over my head. An appointment for an angiogram was scheduled, and explanations of procedures and requirements for us as her parents were added to my spinning brain. As I tried to digest all the information I was receiving in one phone call, I realized they were preparing for the possibility of surgery.

Our prayers were getting more earnest as we progressed through an EEG (brain scan looking for seizure activity) and more doctor visits. We desired healing for our baby so she could live a normal life. Our faith in God came into play as we tried to resign ourselves to His will. Friends, family, and acquaintances all joined us in prayer.

We owned a bulk food store, and many local non-Mennonite folks knew us. We had become good friends with some Christians from a local church. When they heard of the circumstances, they asked if they could have a prayer meeting to lay hands on Judy and pray for her healing. Although the church we attended did not generally do this, we appreciated their sincerity and faith in God, so we agreed to it.

The evening came when we gathered at their church with their pastor and some of the members who knew us. They took turns praying and claimed God’s healing for Judy because they “knew” it was His will to heal her. They specifically asked that the doctors wouldn’t find anything when they did the angiogram. Then they asked us to pray. Although not used to praying out loud, particularly in front of other people, we had confidence that God could heal our baby and wanted to do our part. We prayed for God’s will and voiced our acceptance of whatever He chose.

The next day, we made the hour-and-a-half drive to Madison Children’s Hospital for the angiogram. The purpose for this test was to identify what was causing her seizures and to find its exact location. After the test, we went home to await the results.

I didn’t want my lack of faith to block my daughter’s healing, and I knew God could heal her, but who was I to tell Him what to do? As I struggled through it, we waited for news from the doctor.

Two days later we got a phone call from the doctor’s office. The nurse on the line told us the angiogram hadn’t shown anything! It seemed to puzzle them. It wasn’t at all what they had expected, and they didn’t understand why they couldn’t find the problem. Praise God! We marveled at the miracle He had wrought.

When we took Judy to her next appointment with the neurosurgeon, I asked him what Judy’s problem was since the angiogram found nothing unusual. He said it appeared she had a small amount of bleeding on her brain, but not to worry about it. I thought that was one of the strangest statements I ever heard. I had always been under the impression that bleeding on the brain is very serious and not to be ignored. But I was pretty sure I knew what had happened and told the doctor about the prayers. His response was noncommittal, and I couldn’t tell what he really thought.

They scheduled Judy for a second doctor’s visit and MRI in six months, which I thought was a little strange, considering that they didn’t think there was anything wrong with her. I wasn’t planning to need that MRI or appointment since I believed God had healed her.

That summer, we weaned her off her seizure medications, and she appeared to be healthy. The six months were almost over, and we believed her problems were behind us.

Then, one week before the scheduled MRI, she had a seizure. What a shock! How could this be? Hadn’t God healed her?? What was happening? I felt betrayed. All I could ask was, “Why?” And now what were we going to do?

Such emotional turmoil and soul-searching! I felt let down and shaken in my faith. I had believed in God and that was finally where I ended up every time when I struggled. Solid as a rock under all the turmoil was the truth that God is, and His ways are far above my understanding. I found at the core of my belief in God a safe place where He knows and has my best interest in mind. And that plan might not include the things I want to happen in my limited earth-view.

What if His plan was higher? What if there was someone we would encounter through our medical journey who needed to see Christ in us? Were we willing to be His witness at the expense of our comfort and an easier life?

Our precious little girl ended up having brain surgery at only three and a half years old. Dealing with seizures, surgery, and countless tests over the years caused us no small amount of stress, but God had and still has a plan, and the “whys” we ask might not be revealed until we see Him face to face.

So, does God always answer prayer? I say yes, He does. Sometimes He says, “Yes,” and we get what we want; sometimes, His answer is“No,” and we do not get what we ask for. Sometimes, He whispers, “Wait”, and in His own time and way, He allows us our heart’s desire. Like a child who trusts his parents, I will leave the answers to my prayers in the hands of our almighty God and trust Him to know what is best for my life.

La oración se apodera del plan de Dios y se convierte en el vínculo entre Su voluntad y su cumplimiento en la tierra. Suceden cosas asombrosas, y se nos concede el privilegio de ser los canales de la oración del Espíritu Santo.

—Elisabeth Elliot

En mayo de 2001, Dios bendijo a nuestra familia con una niña. Esta bebé creó mucha emoción mientras la noticia se difundía como reguero de pólvora. “¿Supiste que los Ivans tuvieron una niña?” Su única hermana tenía 14 años, y los últimos cinco bebés habían sido varones. Una bebé tan especial merecía un nombre especial. La llamamos Judith Irene por su abuela y la llamábamos Judy para abreviar.

Las primeras 24 horas después del nacimiento, Judy gimoteó y chilló casi continuamente. “Está disgustada por haber nacido”, bromeé. Después de ese primer día se asentó en una rutina normal de bebé sin señal de algo fuera de lo común.

Una mañana, cuando Judy tenía aproximadamente 18 meses, yo estaba en la sala haciendo mis devocionales personales. Ella estaba en la cocina contigua cuando escuchamos un ruido extraño: un rascar-tac rítmico. Miré con curiosidad a Ivan. “¿Qué es ese ruido?” Con las cejas levantadas, se encogió de hombros. Cuando los sonidos continuaron, me dio curiosidad y me levanté de la mecedora para ir hacia la fuente del ruido. Una sospecha inquietante se asomó en el fondo de mi mente y fue creciendo con cada paso que daba. Cuando entré en la cocina, Judy yacía en el suelo, convulsionando rítmicamente. Nunca había visto a nadie tener una convulsión antes, pero de alguna manera, lo supe al instante. ¡Está teniendo una convulsión!

“¿Llamamos al 911?” Ivan se dirigió al teléfono. Dudé. Como Ivan era bombero, teníamos un escáner de emergencias en la casa. Después de haber escuchado innumerables llamados a lo largo de los años y sabiendo que a veces la ambulancia podía tardar en responder, no me sentía tranquila esperando en casa mientras nuestra hija convulsionaba.

“Llevémosla.” No estaba dispuesta a quedarme sentada y esperar hasta que llegara ayuda.

Judy seguía convulsionando. Ivan la levantó del suelo y me la entregó para poder sacar sus llaves. Sosteniendo a Judy contra mí, me dirigí hacia la puerta. “Trae mis zapatos”, grité por encima del hombro mientras bajaba apresurada las escaleras del porche descalza y me dirigía hacia la camioneta estacionada en la entrada inferior. Ivan me adelantó, abrió la puerta para mí y corrió hacia el lado del conductor. Al bajar la corta y empinada colina, mis pies resbalaron por el rocío de la mañana y quedé a medio camino debajo de la camioneta con una pierna hacia adelante y la otra doblada hacia atrás bajo mí. Por un instante pensé que me había roto la pierna, pero después de uno o dos segundos aturdida, me puse de pie, reuní mi precioso bulto y forcejeé para subirme a la camioneta. Judy todavía convulsionaba y, peor aún, ya no respiraba correctamente. La saliva se acumulaba en las comisuras de su boca, convirtiéndose en espuma. ¡Oh, mi bebé! ¿Qué le pasa? ¿Se va a morir? Es asombroso cuántos pensamientos pueden cruzar por la mente en una situación así. ¿Por qué, oh por qué Ivan no conduce más rápido? ¡No está respirando! Eché un vistazo al velocímetro. Estaba apuntando hacia la derecha. Oh, iba rápido. Con todo mi cuerpo y mi mente, deseé con todas mis fuerzas que estuviéramos en el hospital.

Teníamos un camino directo al hospital, y Ivan detuvo la camioneta junto a la entrada de urgencias. Salté del vehículo con mi bebé, le grité por encima del hombro que trajera mis zapatos y corrí hacia la puerta de emergencias. Una enfermera salía justo a la vuelta de la esquina y casi le arrojé a mi preciosa bebé entre los sorprendidos brazos. “¡Está teniendo una convulsión!” alcancé a decir. La enfermera miró a Judy, se dio la vuelta y corrió por el pasillo con la niña en sus brazos y yo siguiéndola a toda prisa. Para cuando llegamos a una sala, Judy finalmente había dejado de convulsionar. Tendida en la camilla, semi-coma, entró en una segunda convulsión, más leve.

Una vez que salió de la segunda convulsión y las cosas se calmaron, el doctor ordenó algunas pruebas. Tras revisar los resultados, el médico decidió que había experimentado una convulsión febril, la que resulta de que la temperatura corporal sube o baja demasiado rápido. Dijo que eran comunes en bebés y niños pequeños y no pareció demasiado preocupado. Mis instintos de madre cuestionaron su diagnóstico, pero yo no era doctora, así que aceptamos lo que dijo.

Esta fue nuestra introducción al mundo de las convulsiones. Unas semanas después tuvo otra convulsión. Y luego otra más. Nuestros padres nos animaron a buscar una segunda opinión. Este segundo médico decidió que Judy debía hacerse una resonancia magnética, aunque el primer doctor seguía manteniendo que solo tenía convulsiones febriles y no tenía prisa por hacer la resonancia. Pasaron varias semanas hasta que la programaron. Al día siguiente de la resonancia nos llamaron desde el consultorio del médico. Habían concertado una cita con un neurocirujano para dos días después. La situación había cambiado de “no hay prisa” a “ustedes estarán ahí, sin discusión”. El neurocirujano dijo que Judy tenía una MAV (malformación arteriovenosa) e intentó explicar qué era eso, pero la mayoría de la información me pasó por encima. Programaron una angiografía, y las explicaciones de los procedimientos y los requisitos para nosotros como padres se sumaron a mi cabeza que daba vueltas. Mientras trataba de digerir toda la información que recibía en una sola llamada, me di cuenta de que se estaban preparando para la posibilidad de una cirugía.

Nuestras oraciones se hicieron más fervientes mientras avanzábamos con un EEG (electroencefalograma en busca de actividad convulsiva) y más visitas al médico. Deseábamos la sanidad de nuestra bebé para que pudiera llevar una vida normal. Nuestra fe en Dios entró en juego mientras tratábamos de someternos a Su voluntad. Amigos, familiares y conocidos se unieron a nosotros en oración.

Teníamos una tienda de alimentos a granel, y mucha gente local no menonita nos conocía. Nos habíamos hecho buenos amigos de algunos cristianos de una iglesia local. Cuando se enteraron de las circunstancias, preguntaron si podían hacer una reunión de oración para imponer manos sobre Judy y orar por su sanación. Aunque la iglesia a la que asistíamos normalmente no hacía eso, apreciamos su sinceridad y fe en Dios, así que accedimos.

La noche llegó y nos reunimos en su iglesia con su pastor y algunos miembros que nos conocían. Se turnaron para orar y reclamaron la sanidad de Judy porque “sabían” que era voluntad de Dios sanarla. Pidieron específicamente que los médicos no encontraran nada cuando hicieran la angiografía. Luego nos pidieron que rezáramos nosotros. Aunque no estábamos acostumbrados a orar en voz alta, especialmente frente a otras personas, teníamos confianza en que Dios podía sanar a nuestra bebé y queríamos hacer nuestra parte. Oramos por la voluntad de Dios y manifestamos nuestra aceptación de lo que Él escogiera.

A la mañana siguiente, hicimos el viaje de una hora y media al Hospital de Niños de Madison para la angiografía. El propósito de esta prueba era identificar qué estaba causando sus convulsiones y encontrar su ubicación exacta. Después de la prueba, regresamos a casa a esperar los resultados.

No quería que mi falta de fe bloqueara la sanidad de mi hija, y sabía que Dios podía sanarla, pero ¿quién era yo para decirle a Él qué hacer? Mientras luchaba con eso, esperamos noticias del médico.

Dos días después recibimos una llamada del consultorio. La enfermera nos dijo que la angiografía no había mostrado nada. ¡Parecía desconcertarlos! No era en absoluto lo que esperaban y no comprendían por qué no podían encontrar el problema. ¡Alabado sea Dios! Nos maravillamos del milagro que Él había obrado.

Cuando llevamos a Judy a su siguiente cita con el neurocirujano, le pregunté cuál era el problema de Judy, ya que la angiografía no había encontrado nada inusual. Dijo que parecía que tenía una pequeña cantidad de sangrado en el cerebro, pero que no nos preocupáramos. Me pareció una de las declaraciones más extrañas que había oído. Siempre había tenido la impresión de que una hemorragia cerebral es algo muy serio y que no debe ignorarse. Pero estaba bastante segura de lo que había pasado y le conté al médico sobre las oraciones. Su respuesta fue poco comprometida, y no pude discernir realmente lo que pensaba.

Programaron otra visita y una resonancia magnética en seis meses, lo cual me pareció extraño, considerando que no creían que hubiera algo malo con ella. Yo no planeaba necesitar esa resonancia ni esa cita porque creía que Dios la había sanado.

Ese verano, la retiramos de sus medicamentos para las convulsiones, y ella parecía estar sana. Los seis meses casi se cumplían y creíamos que sus problemas habían quedado atrás.

Entonces, una semana antes de la resonancia programada, tuvo una convulsión. ¡Qué choque! ¿Cómo podía ser esto? ¿No la había sanado Dios? ¿Qué estaba pasando? Me sentí traicionada. Todo lo que pude preguntar fue: “¿Por qué?” ¿Y ahora qué íbamos a hacer?

¡Qué tumulto emocional y examen de conciencia! Me sentí defraudada y sacudida en mi fe. Había confiado en Dios y eso era finalmente a lo que llegaba cada vez que luchaba. Tan sólido como una roca en medio de todo el tumulto estaba la verdad de que Dios existe y Sus caminos están muy por encima de mi entendimiento. Encontré en el núcleo de mi creencia en Dios un lugar seguro donde Él conoce y busca mi bien. Y ese plan podría no incluir las cosas que yo quiero que sucedan en mi limitada perspectiva terrenal.

¿Y si Su plan era superior? ¿Y si había alguien que encontraríamos a lo largo de nuestro camino médico que necesitara ver a Cristo en nosotros? ¿Estaríamos dispuestos a ser Su testimonio a costa de nuestra comodidad y de una vida más fácil?

Nuestra preciosa niña terminó sometiéndose a una cirugía cerebral con solo tres años y medio. Lidiar con las convulsiones, la cirugía y las incontables pruebas a lo largo de los años nos causó no poca angustia, pero Dios tenía y aún tiene un plan, y los “porqués” que preguntamos quizás no se revelen hasta que lo veamos cara a cara.

Entonces, ¿Dios siempre responde la oración? Yo digo que sí, Él lo hace. A veces dice “Sí”, y obtenemos lo que queremos; a veces su respuesta es “No”, y no recibimos lo que pedimos. A veces susurra “Espera”, y en Su propio tiempo y manera, nos permite el deseo de nuestro corazón. Como un niño que confía en sus padres, dejaré las respuestas a mis oraciones en las manos de nuestro Dios todopoderoso y confiaré en que Él sabe qué es lo mejor para mi vida.

Someone once said “When hope is alive, the night is less dark, the solitude less deep, and fear less acute.” When I worked in a prison as an assistant chaplain, I would sit with the condemned men and listen as they talked of their plight. Almost without exception, all spoke of hoping to get out of prison one day. Even if they had a life sentence, they hoped to get out.

I have spoken to people who do not confess to be born again, but still hope to go to heaven. These people dare not leave off hoping. Their hope is based upon their own hope! A diet on that kind of hope is a slim diet for sure! This reasoning reminds me of Jesus' words in John 10:1-2 about entering the sheepfold. “But he that entereth in by the door is the shepherd of the sheep.” People build their hope for heaven on many shaky things. Some base their hope on having been baptized in a certain church. Some hope in their church membership. Some people hope in their good works, while still others hope in their hope. The Bible, however, says, “. . . except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John 3:3).

There is a true hope and a false hope. The false hope is “climbing up some other way,” but true hope is “he that entereth in by the door.”

“For we are saved by hope: but hope that is seen is not hope: for what a man seeth, why doth he yet hope for?” (Romans 8:24). This word hope means “with anticipation or great expectation.” Could we say that we are saved by great expectation? Yes, we can. “Labour not for the meat which perisheth, but for that meat which endureth unto everlasting life, which the Son of man shall give unto you: for him hath God the Father sealed” (John 6:27). This seems to be a contradiction of sorts. Are we not saved by grace? Yes, we are saved by grace through faith (Ephesians 2:8). Then what is this being saved by hope and laboring for the “meat which endureth unto everlasting life”?

“Then they said unto him, what shall we do, that we might work the works of God?” Jesus answered and said unto them, “this is the work of God, that ye believe on him whom he hath sent” (John 6:28-29). It is only by grace that we are saved, but as this passage suggests, grace sets a condition. The condition of grace is that we believe on Him. Another condition of salvation is repentance (Mark 1:15), while another is cross-bearing. “Whosoever will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross and follow me” (Mark 8:34).

Everything we would do for Christ, whether believing, repenting, or cross-bearing, is by grace. Whatever we have, or do, is because of Him. We do not work for our salvation, for Christ Himself said, “It is finished.” We have nothing to hope for if we do not meet the conditions of our salvation. Once we receive the Lord Jesus as Saviour, then “hope maketh not ashamed” (Romans 5:5).

As Christ becomes alive in us, we love Him and choose to obey Him. Jesus becomes more precious to us as we mature in our Christian life. As our relationship grows, our expectation grows as well. The more we get to know Him, the more we look forward to being in His presence. As our anticipation of seeing Him grows, we try to do all things possible to please Him. Our great eagerness keeps us from becoming weary, thus, “we are saved by hope.”

Is your hope like the one who “climbeth up some other way,” or like, “he that entereth in by the door”? Do you have a basis for your hope or is it an empty hope that has no foundation?

I trust you are growing up “. . . into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ” (Ephesians 4:15).

I hope you might grow just a little more, so your expectation of seeing Christ might grow as well. The testimony of this expectation is, “. . . in this we groan, earnestly desiring to be clothed upon with our house which is from heaven” (2 Corinthians 5:2).

Кто‑то однажды сказал: «Когда живёт надежда, ночь становится менее тёмной, одиночество — менее глубоким, а страх — менее острым». Когда я работал помощником капеллана в тюрьме, я сидел с приговорёнными к смертной казни и слушал, как они говорили о своей беде. Почти без исключения все говорили о надежде однажды выйти на свободу. Даже если у них был пожизненный срок, они надеялись выйти.

Я разговаривал с людьми, которые не признаются, что рождены свыше, но всё же надеются попасть в небо. Эти люди не смеют прекратить надеяться. Их надежда основана на их собственной надежде! Такая надежда — скудная пища, без сомнения. Эта мысль напоминает мне слова Иисуса в Иоанна 10:1–2 о входе в овчарню. «Но который входит дверью, тот и пастырь овец». Люди строят свою надежду на небе на многих шатких основаниях. Кто‑то основывает надежду на том, что был крещён в определённой церкви. Кто‑то надеется на своё церковное членство. Некоторые надеются на свои добрые дела, другие — надеются на собственную надежду. Однако Библия говорит: «...если кто не родится свыше, не может увидеть Царства Божия» (Иоанна 3:3).

Существует истинная надежда и ложная надежда. Ложная надежда — это «взбираться другим путём», а истинная надежда — это «тот, кто входит дверью».

«Ибо мы спасены надеждою; но надежда, увиденная, уже не есть надежда; ибо кто видит, чего ещё надеется?» (Римлянам 8:24). Слово «надежда» здесь означает «с ожиданием или с великой надеждой». Можем ли мы сказать, что мы спасены великой надеждой? Да, можем. «Не трудитесь за тленную пищу, но за ту пищу, которая остаётся в вечную жизнь, которую Сын Человеческий даст вам; ибо Сына Человеческого запечатал Отец Бог» (Иоанна 6:27). Это кажется некоторым родом противоречия. Разве мы не спасены по благодати? Да, мы спасены благодатью через веру (Ефесянам 2:8). Тогда что значит быть спасённым надеждой и трудиться за «пищу, которая остаётся в вечную жизнь»?

«Тогда они сказали Ему: что нам делать, чтобы творить дела Божии? Иисус ответил им: это — дело Божие, чтобы веровать в Того, Кого Он послал» (Иоанна 6:28–29). Только по благодати мы спасаемся, но, как показывает этот отрывок, благодать ставит условие. Условие благодати — веровать в Него. Ещё одно условие спасения — покаяние (Марк 1:15), а также несение креста. «Если кто хочет идти за Мною, отвергнись себя, и возьми крест свой, и следуй за Мною» (Марк 8:34).

Всё, что мы делаем для Христа — будь то вера, покаяние или ношение креста — происходит по благодати. Всё, что у нас есть или что мы делаем, — из‑за Него. Мы не трудимся ради нашего спасения, потому что Сам Христос сказал: «Совершилось». У нас нет надежды, если мы не выполняем условия нашего спасения. Как только мы принимаем Господа Иисуса как Спасителя, тогда «надежда не постыжает» (Римлянам 5:5).

Когда Христос оживает в нас, мы любим Его и выбираем слушаться Его. Иисус становится для нас дороже по мере того, как мы созреваем в христианской жизни. По мере роста наших взаимоотношений растёт и наше ожидание. Чем больше мы познаём Его, тем сильнее мы стремимся быть в Его присутствии. По мере возрастания нашего предвкушения увидеть Его мы стараемся делать всё возможное, чтобы угодить Ему. Наше большое рвение не даёт нам утомиться, таким образом «мы спасаемся надеждою».

Ваша надежда похожа на ту, кто «взбирается другим путём», или на ту, «кто входит дверью»? Есть ли у вашей надежды основание, или это пустая надежда без фундамента?

Надюсь, вы возрастаете «...в Нём во всём, который есть глава, Христос» (Ефесянам 4:15).

Надеюсь, вы могли бы ещё немного возрасти, чтобы ваше ожидание увидеть Христа тоже увеличилось. Свидетельство об этом ожидания: «...в том и стону, томясь желанием облечься в дом наш, который от небес» (2 Коринфянам 5:2).
